content.text:
## Recommendation: Letter B

**Clarity — B.** B leads with the numbers the board will be asked about, then explains the quarter in three signposted points. It does the small translation work a non-specialist needs: it defines "gross of fees" inline, spells out what the policy index actually contains, and gives the 25% fixed income target so the reader can see that 27.5% is *slightly over*, not floating free. It also says why not selling equities mattered ("long-term investments were left undisturbed") rather than leaving the reader to infer it.

Letter A buries performance in the fourth paragraph, refers to "our comparison index" without ever saying what it is, and says fixed income "remains within our strategic parameters" without naming the parameter — the reader is asked to take the reassurance on trust. "Treasury securities taken advantage of during recent yield spikes" is a garbled construction the board chair will have to re-read.

**Tone — B.** The tone note is the deciding factor: this is read into the minutes of the April 28 board meeting. B is formatted as a document of record — firm block, date, addressee with title, salutation that includes the board — and closes by referencing the meeting and offering to take questions beforehand. That is exactly right for a formal board.

A reads like a letter to an individual client and drifts promotional in a setting where restraint is wanted: "our team successfully executed a grant distribution" (a routine payment, framed as an achievement), "comfortably inside," "remains strong," and "We are pleased to inform you" attached to a fee change. Even a fee *reduction* reads better stated plainly, as B does, than announced with pleasure. A also repeatedly says "our" payout target and "our" fixed income allocation — the assets and the 5% obligation are the Foundation's, and that possessive will sound off when read aloud to the board.

**Overall — B**, and not on length; B's extra words are the definitions and targets that do the clarifying work, not padding. A is competent and would not embarrass anyone, but B is the one I would want in the minutes.

input.reason: B is clearer: it leads with performance, defines "gross of fees" inline, states the composition of the policy index, and names the 25% fixed income target so the 27.5% figure is interpretable. A withholds those reference points ("our comparison index," "within our strategic parameters") and buries returns in the fourth paragraph, with one garbled clause about Treasuries and yield spikes. B also fits the tone notes better: it is formatted as a document of record (firm block, date, addressee with title, salutation to the chair and board) and closes by referencing the April 28 meeting, which suits a letter read into the minutes. A reads as a letter to an individual and drifts promotional — "successfully executed a grant distribution," "comfortably," "remains strong," and "pleased to inform you" on a fee change — and uses "our" for the Foundation's payout obligation and assets. B's advantage is substantive clarity and register, not length.
